newsitem.title: UK: Ex-SFA head says regulators must share information.
newsitem.headline: Ex-SFA head says regulators must share information.

text.p: World financial regulators would do better to pool their information using internet technology than try to set up a global supervisory body, according to the former head of a top British financial watchdog.

Christopher Sharples, ex-chairman of Britain's Securities and Futures Authority (SFA), said this week the very technology which threatened to create problems in global securities markets should be used to build an international database for regional supervisory bodies.

"Technically speaking it would be a 'no-brainer'," Sharples, now chairman of software company Datastream, told a conference in London. "It will be easier to to get regulators to share data than to get someone else to come in and supervise on an international level."

A trend towards globalisation in financial services and amalgamation of banks is fuelling demand for a unified global regulatory body to avoid further incidents of the 'rogue trading' which hit Barings and Daiwa banks.
But Sharples said a better and more realistic solution against malpractice would be a database, accessible electronically by regulators around the world, with agreed terms on use and confidentiality.
"Sharing information is preferable to abrogating responsibility to someone else," he said.
Sharples, who was SFA's chairman at the time of the Barings scandal, said the bank's collapse could have been saved by closer collaboration between the different regulatory bodies.

"Had we in London had access to information from other jurisdictions, I would like to think we might have been able to take pre-emptive action," he told the conference, which focussed on the impact of globalisation of securities markets.
Former Ontario Securities Commission Chairman, Ed Waitzer, agreed that the focus should be on how regulators did their job rather than how they were organised.
He did not rule out the setting up of a global body at some stage, but said he it was unlikely to happen in the near future.
Sharples added: "I can't imagine anyone would be daft enough to take on the job of global regulator anyway."
